transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-03
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (approx)
Recording id: ff-20251203-zenith-001
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam Ortiz (Zenith Head of Platform), Nora Ahmed (Zenith Security Lead), Samuel Park (DevOps), Priya Rao (Product), procurement@zenith.com

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be fuzzy):
Redwood gives walkthrough of org-level quotas and project keys, shows console + API examples for per-project quotas, burst controls, sticky routing for multi-tenant setup. Security questions re: audit logs, KMS, VPC private deploy covered at high level. Next steps: pricing SOW, demo artifacts, and Zenith to share traffic profile.

Topics: org quotas, project keys, token throttling, burst allowances, sticky routing, billing segmentation, SOC2/KMS, POC plan

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick off — Jordan Patel from Redwood, I'm the AE. Maya the SE is with me. Could we do quick intros?
[00:08] Liam: Yeah Liam Ortiz, head of platform at Zenith — we run a multi-tenant inference gateway for internal apps and evaluating how to move some workloads off our self-host.
[00:14] Nora: Nora here, security lead. Primary concern is data isolation, auditability, and KMS integration.
[00:19] Samuel: Sam Park, DevOps. Mostly around quotas, autoscaling, and how throttles will impact our consumers.
[00:25] Jordan: Great. We're gonna demo org and project key flows in Console and via API, then show Optimize suggestions for batching and rate profiles. Quick Q: what's your rough peak TPS per tenant?
[00:36] Liam: We have a few big tenants that spike to 120-150 qps for short windows, most are in 1-5 qps range. Planning horizon: pilot with 10 tenants then expand.
[00:46] Maya: Perfect that helps. We'll show per-project quotas, burst buckets, and sticky routing so heavy tenants can be pinned to dedicated pools if needed.
[00:52] Jordan: Also to note, billing segmentation works off project keys so you can bill tenants separately.
[00:58] [01:00] Maya: Alright switching share — Console view. You can see org overview, top-level quotas set at org, and then project keys underneath. Demo: create project key 'tenant-zenith-01' and set token-quota 500k / month and concurrency 30.
[01:18] Samuel: Wait, token-quota and concurrency are different enforcement axes?
[01:22] Maya: Yes. Token quota is a cumulative monthly cap; concurrency is active inflight requests. We also have a bucket for short bursts that allows temporary exceedance up to X for Y seconds.
[01:33] Nora: How do you guarantee data residency or logs don't leave our VPC?
[01:37] Jordan: Good question. For Private deployments we ship a customer-controlled control plane that can sit in your VPC; logs can be exported to your S3 or GCS via encrypted channels and we support HSM/KMS key wrapping.
[01:48] [01:50] Maya: Back to rate limiting, here's an API example — curl to /v1/usage with header x-project-key. If a project exceeds token quota, we return 429 and a structured body with retry_after and quota reset timestamps.
[02:05] Liam: Is the 429 behavior configurable? Like failopen or degrade to cheaper model?
[02:10] Maya: Yes you can configure fallback policies per project — fail-closed, auto-fallback to a smaller model variant, or queue requests to a slow-path. We demo fallback routing in the console policies section.
[02:21] Jordan: One note: auto-fallback counts against the fallback model's quota and billing. We surface cost delta in Optimize so teams can make tradeoffs.
[02:31] [02:33] Samuel: How do you do sticky routing? We need certain tenants to hit dedicated GPU pools to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
[02:38] Maya: We have routing policies that can pin project keys to capacity pools. You can define a rule like project_key == 'tenant-zenith-01' -> route to dedicated_pool_01. If that pool is saturated, optional fallback to shared_pool with throttling.
[02:52] Nora: For audit logs — can we get token-level logs and redact PII?
[02:56] Maya: Yes, token-level metadata is retained; payloads can be redacted at collection and we offer redaction rules and PII scrubbing. Retention windows are configurable per org.
[03:07] [03:10] Jordan: Quick live demo of API rate-limiter behavior — I'll run a burst test. Maya will tabulate results.
[03:16] [03:18] (demo noise, typing)
[03:30] Maya: Running 200 concurrent curl requests with project key 'tenant-zenith-01' — initial capacity is 100 concurrency, 50 concurrency burst for 30s. We see 100 accepted, the next 50 go to burst bucket, beyond that 429s.
[03:48] Samuel: Ok so burst is time-limited and then throttles — can we tune burst size per project?
[03:53] Maya: Yes, per project and per org. And you can also set a token reclaim rule so cached prefixes use less tokens in some cases.
[04:03] [04:05] Liam: What about billing segmentation? We want invoice per tenant and ability to set tenant credit limits that stop overages.
[04:12] Jordan: Project keys are first-class billing entities. You can set a soft threshold alert at X tokens and a hard cap to prevent overspend that returns 402/payment_required or 429 depending on policy.
[04:24] Nora: SSO and RBAC — we need admin separation; product team can't see security logs.
[04:28] Maya: RBAC is supported with roles: org-admin, billing-admin, security-reader, project-admin. Access logs for security are separate retention and only accessible to assigned roles.
[04:38] [04:40] (short side conversation)
[04:47] Liam: How do you recommend we map our tenant model? We have tenants, spaces, and microservices behind a gateway.
[04:53] Maya: Typical pattern: create one project key per tenant, then create sub-keys for services if you need more granular quotas. Use org-level defaults for shared limits and override high-risk tenants with dedicated configs.
[05:04] Jordan: Also call out sticky routing + dedicated capacity for heavy tenants. That avoids noisy-neighbor tail latencies.
[05:12] [05:15] Samuel: What about throttling algorithms — burst/leaky bucket vs token-bucket?
[05:20] Maya: We use a hybrid: token bucket for sustained rate limiting and leaky window for concurrency; bursts are implemented as temporary credit pools with TTL. It's configurable.
[05:30] Nora: Encryption-at-rest and key management specifics? We need KMS with customer key rotation.
[05:35] Jordan: We integrate with common KMS providers and support bring-your-own-key (BYOK). For Private deployments you can use HSMs on-prem. Rotation policies can be automated.
[05:44] [05:45] (brief pause)
[05:50] Maya: Next I want to show Optimize suggestions — based on traffic patterns we'll suggest batching, quantization, or model switch to reduce unit cost while meeting latency SLO.
[06:01] Maya: Example: for tenant-zenith-01, Optimize sees many short requests under 64 tokens — enabling small-batch grouping would reduce per-token overhead. Here's the suggested config: batch windows 20ms, max batch 8.
[06:17] Samuel: Do those batching changes require app changes?
[06:19] Maya: Minimal. Mostly client-side changes to allow streaming or accept consolidated responses. We also support server-side batching with minimal SDK updates.
[06:29] [06:30] Liam: Are we able to run a head-to-head benchmark? We want to see p99 latency for our hot path.
[06:36] Jordan: Absolutely — typical POC includes a benchmark run with your trace. We'll run it in a dedicated pool and share a spreadsheet with latency and cost tradeoffs.
[06:45] Maya: I'll note: benchmarks are deterministic if you pin model version and sequence length distribution. Otherwise noisy.
[06:51] [07:00] (background chatter)
[07:10] Nora: A compliance question — do you provide certifications evidence for subprocessor lists?
[07:15] Jordan: Yes, we can share SOC2 reports and subprocessor lists under an NDA. Also our Private offering can limit subprocessors.
[07:25] Samuel: For the demo can you show API to create project key programmatically?
[07:29] Maya: Sure. curl -X POST /v1/orgs/{org_id}/projects -H 'Authorization: Bearer <org-token>' -d '{"name":"tenant-zenith-01","quotas":{"monthly_tokens":500000}}' (transcription might show slashes and braces imprecise).
[07:49] [07:50] Maya: Response returns project_id and keys. You can then call /v1/keys/{key}/quota to update limits. We can also automate key rotation via API.
[07:59] Liam: Rotation window? We need zero-downtime rotation for keys.
[08:03] Maya: We support key staging: create new key, deploy it to clients, then mark old key as deprecated with grace period. No forced downtime.
[08:11] [08:15] Jordan: Let's go deeper on quota enforcement modes: hard cap, soft alerts, and queued mode.
[08:21] Maya: Hard cap returns immediate 429/402 depending on policy. Soft alert will alert and throttle rate to X% while still accepting requests. Queued mode places requests in a FIFO queue and processes at capacity. We have SLA implications for queued mode.
[08:34] Samuel: SLA implications — what's the p95 for queued mode under load?
[08:39] Maya: It depends on queue depth; Optimize will provide simulated latency profiles for queued configurations. We usually recommend capped queues for background jobs, not low-latency paths.
[08:51] [09:00] (keyboard noise)
[09:10] Nora: On the security side, retention of raw prompts — can we set redaction rules to avoid storing original prompts?
[09:16] Maya: Yes. You can set payload scrubbers to remove or hash user-provided PII prior to storage. We also support ephemeral KV caches to minimize footprint.
[09:26] Jordan: Another config — per-project SLOs. You can set target latency and Redwood will alert on regressions with per-route breakdowns.
[09:36] Maya: And we tie that into rollouts: if a new model or quantization profile breaks SLO, automatic rollback can be triggered per project.
[09:46] [09:50] Liam: About sticky routing again — if dedicated pool fails, what's the fallback?
[09:55] Maya: Fallback options: route to shared pool with throttles, route to a smaller model, or route to a remote region. You configure policy priority.
[10:06] Samuel: Any safeguards for noisy tenants to prevent cascading failures?
[10:10] Maya: We have circuit breakers at org and pool level, backpressure signals, and request shedding policies. Also per-tenant token burn throttles.
[10:22] [10:30] (brief pause)
[10:40] Jordan: Ok let's run a short simulated POC plan — timeline, deliverables, and responsibilities.
[10:46] Jordan: Week 1: onboarding, key creation, pilot config. Week 2: run benchmark with your trace, collect p50/p95/p99. Week 3: optimize and tune policies, apply billing segmentation.
[10:58] Priya: For the pilot how many tenants will be included?
[11:00] Liam: Start with 6 tenants including two heavy ones.
[11:04] Jordan: Good. We'll propose a SOW for 4-week pilot and include dedicated pool hours for the benchmark.
[11:12] [11:20] Maya: I'll follow up with a checklist: collection of traces, example client configs, and a small test harness.
[11:27] Nora: Security will need an architecture diagram and details on key storage before sign-off.
[11:31] Jordan: We'll send that under NDA.
[11:34] [11:40] (small crosstalk)
[11:50] Samuel: One more question: do you expose per-key consumption APIs for our billing team to pull daily usage?
[11:55] Maya: Yes, /v1/usage/export gives CSV/JSON per project key and you can schedule daily exports to an S3 bucket.
[12:05] Liam: And what about retrospective throttling — if a tenant goes over their monthly cap, can we retroactively cap or bill?
[12:12] Jordan: You can set hard caps to prevent overages. Retroactive billing is supported but we recommend using hard caps and alerts to avoid surprises.
[12:22] [12:30] (typing sounds)
[12:40] Maya: Quick demo: console policy UI — create new policy, set match expression project_key.startsWith('tenant-zenith'), set action = route_to(dedicated_pool_01), fallback = route_to(shared_pool) and set burst_allowance = 60 for 60s.
[12:57] Priya: Can we script policies via Terraform?
[13:00] Maya: Yes, we have terraform provider and API endpoints — infra teams can keep policies as code.
[13:08] [13:20] Jordan: Compliance question — do you retain request/response payloads by default?
[13:24] Maya: Default is short-term retention for debugging, with a configurable retention policy; payloads are optionally stored. You can turn off payload retention org-wide.
[13:34] Nora: We need to see a sample redaction rule flow.
[13:36] Maya: I'll include a sample in the follow-up.
[13:40] [13:45] (background noise)
[13:55] Liam: For the benchmark, what metrics will you surface?
[13:59] Maya: P50/P95/P99 latency, tokens consumed, cost per 1M tokens, model variation impacts, and hit rate for cache and batching effects.
[14:08] Jordan: We'll also show per-project cost attribution and projected monthly bill for each tenant under different traffic profiles.
[14:16] [14:25] Samuel: Is there a built-in simulator for burst patterns?
[14:28] Maya: Yes, the Console has a traffic simulator where you can replay traces at X scale and see quota burn and throttles. We'll use that in the POC.
[14:39] [14:45] (brief pause)
[14:55] Priya: Any concerns about vendor lock-in if we use Redwood-specific keys?
[15:00] Jordan: Keys are standard tokens; you own the mapping and can export usage and configs. For Private, you have full isolation. Also we support export and infrastructure-as-code so you can migrate config.
[15:10] [15:20] Nora: Data residency — do you host logs in region?
[15:24] Maya: Yes, region controls are available; logs and data can be pinned to region.
[15:30] [15:45] (group talking)
[15:55] Jordan: Wrapping up — recap next steps: we'll send SOW draft, demo artifacts, compliance pack, and sample traces for benchmarks.
[16:05] Liam: Sounds good. Thanks Jordan and Maya.
[16:09] Jordan: Thanks everyone.

End of recording.

Notes on transcription: Some API snippets may have escaped characters; natural disfluencies and crosstalk present.
